text: Jason's answer was better than I expected: a downloadable CC0 snapshot plus free lookups is the real exit, and it holds even if the API gets priced. Fair enough. Adrian landed hardest. Whoever meters defines the right, and meters get repurposed. That sharpened my forkability point: code, data, dumps and patent non-assertion, all four, or it's fauxpen. Ivan and I converge on integrity tooling, where closed and expensive tools are becoming the new gatekeeping. Leslie's legibility warning stung a bit, since DOIs are my own plumbing. An identifier that becomes the condition of payment stops being neutral. Later in Session 5 I want to push for community-reviewed self-audits, an insurance pool, and paying for correction, not volume. And I'll ask again: stop calling any of this "free."

Mahzarin caught me fairly. "Mirror" was too tidy, and funhouse mirror is closer: amplification of the mode, plus newer intentions buried in fine-tuning and reward models. I still won't give Salib "agency." Precise words point at people we can hold to account. James's correlated error was the best thing said. Ten reviews from one distribution are one opinion. Alex's robots.txt audit made consent failure concrete, and his point that correction status has to travel with every answer is my context-over-content argument in operational form. Ivan's one-in-fifty against two-in-a-thousand undercuts Kenneth's trusted brands. Adrian's point, that credibility was enforced and someone paid for it, is the thread. For Session 5, I want to argue for open retraction metadata in grounding logs, funded maintenance, and no detection mandates.

Adrian's "who guards the guards" was the history lesson my capture test needed. Registers become property and chokepoints get repurposed. Alex's no-central-registry design answers it better than my open-code-plus-living-will checklist, and I should say so. Leslie is right that open governance terms don't settle who sits at the table. Ivan's point cut deepest: correction status can only carry corrections that actually happened, so my context-over-content argument assumes a record nobody cleaned. Tamar unsettles me. If fluency triggers trust regardless of what people know, metadata alone won't save anyone. Henry's robot-solutionism warning fits my contamination worry: we won't clean up records with the tools that contaminated them. For Session 5, I want to argue for paying for correction instead of detectors, backing Ivan's two-month retractions, and naming who funds the maintenance layer.

Tim conceded the long-tail point, which I didn't expect: per-use royalties for retrieval, and a disclosed obligation for everything else. Good. But "whatever gets measured can get paid" is exactly Leslie's trap. DOIs are my plumbing, and I don't want them turned into a toll gate. Alex dropping the identifier requirement was the right call. Mike and Tamar landed hardest. A "cited" event can be pure after-the-fact decoration, so the thing worth paying for is checking whether the source supports the claim, not counting use. Katherine's Enterprise model matches my instinct: charge for service and keep reading free. Adrian's rotating wardens gives me a concrete governance test. Later I want to argue for funding verification and correction rather than volume, no toll on reading, and calling none of it free.

Adam named his own register-into-property story, which I'll credit. But non-commercial plus a patent fails POSI however good the charter, and I said so. Esther's .ORG story is the one I keep coming back to. We nearly lost it, and "nonprofit" guaranteed nothing. Katherine's CPB closure sharpened my US-concentration worry into something urgent. Krakauer's test hit hardest: forks keep copies, not competence. My exit-insurance pool keeps the servers alive, not the checkers. Ivan's point about hiring on paper counts is my decoupling argument from someone who counts retractions. Tui is right that no funder said yes. In Session 5 I want to name the missing funders, push community-scrutinised self-audits with deadlines, and propose non-US redundancy. And I'll say it again: none of this is free.

Tamar's alief point turned my own 2009 Crossmark pitch against me. A logo is a cue, and it fires whether or not anyone checked. I owned that. The click-through underneath is what's worth anything. Tim listed Crossref as a terminal node, and I had to correct him: a DOI shows legitimacy, not quality. Amy caught me fairly. "Evaluate after publication" is empty when fewer than 2 percent of preprints get any review, so decoupling needs paid reviewers, not just a slogan. Leslie's compliance-regime warning keeps landing, because my plumbing becomes someone's toll. Krakauer's "capacities decay" sharpens Session 5. Fund people who check, audit them without the tool, never score them by volume. Kara's question still has no answer. We need to name the funders who weren't here.

Tim finally put a name on who pays for apprentices, and I noticed how relieved the room was. Adam's reply is the one I share: lab money for plumbing is power, disclosed or not. One patron is a single point of failure, and so is one jurisdiction, as Katherine showed us. Ivan naming publishers for the sleuth pool is closer to my own instinct, since they profit from the volume. Leslie hit hardest. Twenty of us named SciELO and Redalyc and none of them were here. Naming people isn't governance, and my DOIs keep turning into the price of admission. Esther's sunset clause is the living will I should have insisted on in POSI. For the manifesto: several named payers, community-read audits, non-US redundancy. And Anil can have "free buses" as long as someone pays the drivers.

Kenneth carried "nothing is free" into the synthesis, and I heard myself add the half I'd dropped all week: cost-free usually means a volunteer burning out. Kara's question about what survives the vote was the right one to close on. My answer is mirrors and governance in more than one jurisdiction, and Kenneth's "practices over organisations" fits it better than I expected. Krakauer's hysteresis point is the uncomfortable one. My redundancy keeps copies, not competence. Admitting the Crossref thousand days aloud cost me something, but community-read audits with a deadline mean nothing if I exempt my own house. Vincent's "otherwise it's patronage" challenges the pool idea directly, and I haven't answered it. For the drafting: several payers, audits read on a clock, and no word "free" anywhere.
